title: Charlie Chaplin and silent cinema
subject: art
description: **Charlie Chaplin** invented the Tramp, a vagrant in a bowler hat, and became the first global movie star. From silent film to sound, he turned laughter into an art.

hero.hook: Before radio and television, a silent tramp made the whole planet laugh.

blocks.text: **Charlie Chaplin** (1889-1977) was the first true global celebrity. In an age of industrial misery, his character **the Tramp**, a dignified and clumsy vagrant, offered a human face. Without a word, he made people laugh and cry in Tokyo, Paris, and New York.
This course follows his path: from the origins of cinema to the masterpieces of the silent era, and then to forced exile. Chaplin was not only a clown. He was a complete author.

Cinema was born from a French invention: the [[Cinematograph]], patented in **1895**, the machine that opens the story of [[The Lumière brothers and early cinema]]. On **December 28, 1895**, at the Grand Café in Paris, the first paying public screening took place. The first films were short documents: workers leaving a factory, a train pulling into a station.

blocks.caption: 1895: cinema becomes a shared spectacle in Paris

blocks.text: Very soon [[Georges Méliès]], a French illusionist, invented fiction and camera tricks. Then the industry organized itself in the United States. **Hollywood** became the capital of dreams, with studios turning out films on an assembly line. That factory is where Chaplin made his name.

Born poor in London in **1889**, Charles Spencer Chaplin grew up between cabarets and workhouses. Trained in the [[music-hall]], he arrived in Hollywood. In **1914**, almost by accident, he put together the costume of **the Tramp**: a bowler hat too small, trousers too wide, a cane, and a mustache.

blocks.caption: The Tramp: a gentleman without a penny, known by his silhouette alone

blocks.text: Chaplin assembled the costume in a few minutes in a studio dressing room, borrowing clothes that were too big and too small from the other actors.

The Tramp is not only funny. He stands for the man who holds on to his dignity in spite of poverty. Chaplin worked in [[Slapstick]], the comedy of falls and blows, but he added a rare feeling to it: tenderness.

In **1927**, sound arrived with *The Jazz Singer*. Chaplin, a cofounder of [[United Artists]], held out. Giving the Tramp a voice would break his universality. So he kept working silent, with *City Lights* (**1931**).

Then history caught up with him. In **1940**, he made *The Great Dictator*, a satire of **Adolf Hitler**. It was his first fully talking picture, shot while the United States was still cautious about Nazism. The clown had become a committed artist.

sections.title: Exile and the legacy of an author

blocks.text: After 1945, the [[Cold War]] and [[McCarthyism]] took hold. Suspected of left-wing views, Chaplin was watched. In **1952**, while he was leaving for Europe, the United States barred him from coming back. He settled in [[Vevey]], Switzerland, for the rest of his life.

events.title: Forced exile
events.detail: Barred from the United States, he left for Switzerland.

blocks.text: Chaplin invented a silent language the whole world could read. A complete author, actor, director, and composer, he proved that popular cinema could also be political and deeply moving.
